newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon cabinet to discuss tight 1997 draft budget.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon cabinet to discuss tight 1997 draft budget.

text.p: Lebanon's government is expected to begin on Wednesday debating a draft 1997 public budget of 6,375 billion Lebanese pounds with a 35.68 percent deficit of income against expenditure, officials said on Tuesday.

The officials confirmed a budget draft published in Beirut newspapers on Tuesday which put next year's total expenditures at 6,375 billion pounds against revenue of 4,100 billion -- a shortfall of 35.68 percent.
This compared with planned 1996 expenditure of 6,458 billion against 4,022 billion income, a 38 percent target deficit.

But finance ministry figures published last week showed that the state budget deficit was 47.8 percent in the first eight months of 1996 alone -- well above the target for the year approved by parliament to keep public finances under control.
In 1995, the final shortfall of income against expenditure was 47 percent compared with a target deficit of 44 percent.
The officials said the cabinet was set to discuss the budget draft on Wednesday and Thursday. The draft will also need parliament's approval.

Acting finance minister Fouad Siniora was quoted on Tuesday by the daily newspaper an-Nahar as saying that the 1996 budget deficit estimates were "negatively affected" by a 17-day Israeli blitz on Lebanon in April.
The onslaught, aimed against pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) guerrillas, killed 200 people and caused extensive damage to infrastructure and businesses, mainly in south Lebanon.

The leftist daily as-Safir said it was almost impossible for the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, who is spearheading Lebanon's postwar revival, to realise the planned 1996 income in the last four months of the year.

Under the 1997 budget draft, the biggest allocation -- 2,700 billion pounds or 42.35 percent of the total -- will go towards debt servicing and interest. This was an increase of about 100 billion over 1996.
About 29 percent of January-August expenditure went for public debt servicing, the finance ministry figures had shown.

Some 2,100 billion pounds in the 1997 draft was allocated to wages and salaries. Defence allocations rose to 732 billion from 1996's 658 billion and education allocations increased to 362 billion from 314 billion.

The public works ministry's share was slashed to 78 billion from 211 billion in 1996. Other cuts were noted in allocations of the housing ministry, three billion from 13, and the transport ministry, 34 billion against 94 billion in 1996.
